messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 68
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Non-profit Worker
  trauma_type: Rape
  pcl5: 76

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Self-Harm: hurt myself physically to release overwhelming feelings, Avoid Being Alone: Being alone in a room or building, Sit With Back to Wall: always sit with back against a wall to see the room
  Threat: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home, Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
  Memory: Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it, Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
  Negative Appraisals: Bad Coper: My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper, Lost Emotions: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again, Outsider: I am permanently an outsider now

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Arjun Patel was sixty when the rape took place in the back storage room of the nonprofit where he spent his days. He had come to believe that the danger arrived as a sudden invasion of the familiar. When the man’s hands found him, the sharp click of the steel door latching behind him, the low groan of the building’s ventilation system, and the abrupt brush of wool against his arm became the precise anchors of what happened. He was certain that the quiet confinement was what mattered most. In the weeks that followed, Arjun navigated his own life with the room’s boundaries still felt. He began avoiding being alone in a room or building, preferring the hum of the office floor to the silence of empty corridors. When he sat in meetings or waited for the evening train, he always positioned himself with his back against the wall, eyes scanning the space. The world moved through him with parallel intensities. Arjun had come to listen for sounds that might mean someone was entering his home, his head tilting toward the hallway long before the doorknob turned. He was on high alert when he heard unexpected or loud sounds, his breath catching as though the storage room walls were closing in. When a colleague patted his shoulder in the breakroom, he reacted with alarm, his body jolting as the touch registered. The memories did not arrive as stories but as physical returns. He knew what had happened to him, yet he was unable to find words to describe it, his tongue pressing against the roof of his mouth. During these episodes, the memory returned with the same pressure he had felt, and he would press a hand to his ribs and thighs, feeling the physical pain bloom in the exact parts that had been bruised. Sometimes, when the quiet of the evening settled, he heard things in his head that he had heard during the frightening event, layered over his own breathing. Over months that stretched into years, Arjun watched his own habits move alongside his perceptions. Divorced for over a decade now, he lived in a small apartment where the routines accumulated without drawing attention. He had come to believe that his reactions since the event showed that he was a lousy coper, that every flinch and every locked door stood as quiet evidence of his fragility. He was certain he would never be able to feel normal emotions again, his heart operating on a different rhythm than those around him. Even within his work at the nonprofit, the open-plan offices and frequent staff gatherings sat alongside his quiet presence, making him feel permanently an outsider to the faster movements of the younger coordinators. When the feelings grew heavy, he hurt himself physically, the sharp sting registering alongside the overwhelming feelings. He maintained these practices in parallel with his daily life. Now, at sixty-eight, Arjun sits in a community clinic waiting room, his back firmly against the plastered wall, his eyes tracking the door. His PCL-5 score of 76 maps the breadth of his alertness, though he does not see it as a diagnosis so much as a record of his present state. He had come to seek help alongside the weight of staying alert, the accumulated habits of years pressing against his ribs. He is most afraid of the sudden touch in a crowded elevator, of the quiet that might mean someone is still in the house, of the day he will realize he has lost the ability to simply be. What he hopes for is not a cure, but a way to exist without constantly bracing for the latch to click. He watches the clock, listens to the low murmur of voices down the hall, and waits, certain that if he keeps his back to the wall and his hands ready, he will be able to step forward.
